scene: Mid-case, volume control. Peak pressure alarm fires.
question: Where is the problem?
why: A big peak-plateau gap with a normal plateau points to resistance, not compliance. Think kinked or bitten tube, secretions, or bronchospasm. Check the circuit, pass a suction catheter, listen for wheeze.
pearl: Peak up alone = airway resistance. Peak AND plateau up = lung or chest wall.
caption:
Peak pressure 40, plateau 18. Is it the tube or the lungs? 🫁

Comment your pick before the answer 👇

A wide gap between peak and plateau means high resistance: kinked or bitten tube, secretions, or bronchospasm. When peak AND plateau rise together, think compliance: mainstem tube, pneumothorax, insufflation, or chest wall.

scene: End of case. Strong hand grip, 5-second head lift.
question: Extubate?
why: Grip and head lift can look normal with a TOF ratio well below 0.9. Residual block raises the risk of aspiration and post-op hypoxemia. Reverse per your plan and confirm a quantitative TOF ratio of 0.9 or more.
pearl: Clinical signs miss residual block. Measure it, don't guess.
caption:
Strong hand grip, 5-second head lift, but the quantitative TOF ratio reads 0.6. Do you pull the tube? 💪

Comment your pick before the answer 👇

Clinical tests miss residual neuromuscular block. A TOF ratio below 0.9 still means weak pharyngeal muscles and higher aspiration and hypoxemia risk. Reverse per your plan and confirm TOFR ≥ 0.9 with quantitative monitoring before extubation.

slides.title: Plateau minus PEEP. The number that predicts lung stress.
slides.sub: Driving pressure and auto-PEEP, in one swipe.

slides.body: It shows tidal volume relative to the lung that is actually open. Lower is generally safer. Many lung-protective targets aim for under about 15 cmH2O.
The next breath starts before the lungs empty. Common with COPD, asthma, fast rates and short expiratory times.

bullets: Expiratory flow doesn't return to zero
Expiratory hold shows PEEP above set
slides.pearl: Sudden hypotension with air trapping? Briefly disconnect and let the patient exhale.

slides.title: Plateau. PEEP. Flow curve.
slides.body: Check all three every time the pressures change.

caption:
Your plateau is fine, but is your driving pressure? 📈

scene: 3 min after the antibiotic. Wheeze, rising peak pressure, flushed skin.
question: First drug?
why: This is anaphylaxis until proven otherwise. Stop the trigger, call for help, 100% O2, fluids, and give epinephrine early. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts. Send a tryptase.
pearl: Antihistamines won't fix the airway or the BP. Epinephrine does.
caption:
Three minutes after the antibiotic: BP 68/34, wheezing, SpO2 falling. What's your first drug? 🚨

Comment your pick before the answer 👇

Treat it as anaphylaxis: stop the trigger, call for help, 100% O2, fluids, and epinephrine early. Antihistamines and steroids are second-line adjuncts. Send a tryptase and refer for allergy testing.
